notes.definition: Corrosion is the destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment. Rusting of iron is an example; both air (oxygen) and water are needed. Corrosion can be prevented by barrier coatings or by sacrificial protection with a more reactive metal.
explanation: Corrosion is the destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment, such as oxygen and water. Rusting is an example of corrosion: iron (and steel, which is mostly iron) reacts with oxygen and water to form rust, which is hydrated iron(III) oxide. Rust is weak and flaky, so it falls away and exposes fresh iron underneath to further corrosion. This is why rusting can eventually destroy a whole iron object. Word equation: iron + oxygen + water → hydrated iron(III) oxide.

Both air and water are necessary for iron to rust. This can be shown with an experiment using three test tubes, each with an iron nail. In tube 1 the nail is in tap water open to the air: it rusts. In tube 2 the nail is in water that has been boiled to remove dissolved air, with a layer of oil on top to stop air dissolving again: it does not rust. In tube 3 the nail is in dry air, with anhydrous calcium chloride to absorb water vapour and a bung to keep out moist air: it does not rust. Salt water speeds up rusting.

Corrosion can be prevented by applying a coating that acts as a barrier, stopping air and water reaching the metal. Examples include greasing or oiling (used on moving parts such as bicycle chains), painting (used on large objects such as bridges and cars) and electroplating (using electrolysis to coat the object with a thin layer of another, less easily corroded metal, such as chromium on taps or tin on food cans). Barrier methods only work while the coating is unbroken: if it is scratched, the iron underneath can rust.

Aluminium is quite a reactive metal, but it does not corrode badly. This is because aluminium has an oxide coating: a thin, tough layer of aluminium oxide forms on its surface and protects the metal underneath from further corrosion. Unlike rust, this layer does not flake off.

Some coatings are reactive and contain a more reactive metal to provide sacrificial protection. For example, zinc is used to galvanise iron: the iron is coated with a layer of zinc. Zinc is more reactive than iron, so if the coating is scratched and the iron is exposed, the zinc reacts (is oxidised) in preference to the iron. The zinc 'sacrifices' itself and corrodes instead of the iron. Blocks of zinc or magnesium are also attached to ship hulls and underground pipelines for the same reason. In terms of electrons, the more reactive metal loses electrons more easily, so it is oxidised instead of the iron.
keyFacts: Corrosion is the destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment.
Rusting is the corrosion of iron and steel; rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide.
Iron needs both air (oxygen) and water to rust.
Experiment: nails in tap water (rusts), boiled water under oil (no rust), dry air with calcium chloride (no rust).
Aluminium has a protective oxide coating that prevents further corrosion.
Sacrificial protection uses a more reactive metal (for example zinc or magnesium) that corrodes instead of iron.
Galvanising is coating iron with zinc; it protects even when scratched.

keyTerms.definition: The destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment.
The corrosion of iron or steel by reaction with oxygen and water, forming hydrated iron(III) oxide.
A coating such as grease, paint or a plated metal that stops air and water reaching the metal.
Using electrolysis to coat an object with a thin layer of another metal.
Attaching or coating a more reactive metal, which is oxidised (corrodes) instead of the metal being protected.
Coating iron or steel with a layer of zinc to provide both a barrier and sacrificial protection.
A drying agent that absorbs water vapour from the air.

equations.name: Rusting
equations.formula: iron + oxygen + water → hydrated iron(III) oxide (rust)

workedExamples.title: Interpreting the rusting experiment
workedExamples.question: Three nails are set up: A in tap water open to air, B in boiled water with oil on top, C in a sealed tube with anhydrous calcium chloride. After a week only A has rusted. Explain what the results show.
steps: A has both air and water, and it rusted.
B has water but no air (boiling removed dissolved air, the oil stops air dissolving): no rust, so air is needed.
C has air but no water (calcium chloride absorbs water vapour): no rust, so water is needed.
workedExamples.answer: Both air (oxygen) and water are needed for iron to rust.

workedExamples.title: Percentage increase in mass on rusting
workedExamples.question: An iron nail has a mass of 2.50 g. After rusting for two weeks its mass is 2.62 g. Calculate the percentage increase in mass and explain why the mass increases.
steps: Mass increases because oxygen and water from the environment have combined with the iron to form rust.
workedExamples.answer: 4.8%; atoms of oxygen (and water) have been added to the iron.

workedExamples.title: Choosing a method of rust prevention
workedExamples.question: Suggest the best method to prevent rusting for (a) a bicycle chain, (b) a steel dustbin, (c) a ship's hull.
steps: (a) Moving parts: paint would crack off, so use oil or grease.
(b) Galvanising with zinc gives a barrier and sacrificial protection if scratched.
(c) Paint plus blocks of zinc or magnesium attached for sacrificial protection, because the hull is in salt water and paint may be damaged.
workedExamples.answer: (a) oil/grease; (b) galvanising; (c) paint with sacrificial zinc or magnesium blocks.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all metals rust.
misconceptions.right: In fact only iron and steel rust; other metals corrode, and the word rust means hydrated iron(III) oxide.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think iron rusts in water alone.
misconceptions.right: In fact both oxygen (air) and water are needed; iron in boiled water under oil does not rust.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think aluminium does not corrode because it is unreactive.
misconceptions.right: In fact aluminium is quite reactive, but a thin, tough oxide layer forms on its surface and protects it.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think galvanising only works as a barrier.
misconceptions.right: In fact zinc also gives sacrificial protection: it is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes instead even when the coating is scratched.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a nail gets lighter when it rusts.
misconceptions.right: In fact the mass increases, because oxygen and water combine with the iron.

realWorld: Galvanised steel is used for dustbins, fences, motorway barriers and car bodies.
Ships and oil rigs have blocks of zinc or magnesium bolted to their hulls as sacrificial anodes.
Food cans are steel electroplated with tin; taps and bike handlebars are chromium plated.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is for separate Chemistry (8462) only.
Corrosion is the destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment; rusting needs both air and water.
Barrier methods: greasing, painting, electroplating. Aluminium is protected by its oxide coating.
Sacrificial protection: a more reactive metal such as zinc (galvanising) is oxidised instead of iron, explained by relative reactivity.
examTips: Use the exact phrase: corrosion is the destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment.
In the rusting experiment, explain the purpose of each control: boiling removes dissolved air, oil stops air dissolving, calcium chloride absorbs water.
For sacrificial protection, always say the metal is MORE reactive than iron, so it is oxidised (loses electrons) instead of iron.
When choosing a prevention method, link it to the object: grease for moving parts, paint for large structures, galvanising or sacrificial blocks where scratches are likely.
Say 'rust' only for iron; for other metals say 'corrode'.
summary: Corrosion: destruction of materials by reaction with substances in the environment.
Iron rusts only when both air and water are present.
Aluminium's oxide layer protects it from further corrosion.
Sacrificial protection: a more reactive metal (zinc, magnesium) corrodes instead of iron.
Galvanised iron is protected even when scratched.

questions.question: What is corrosion?
options: The melting of metals at high temperature
The destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment
The dissolving of metals in water
The wearing away of materials by friction
markScheme: 1 mark: destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment
questions.explanation: Corrosion is a chemical change. Friction wear is a physical process, not corrosion.

questions.question: Which two substances must both be present for iron to rust?
markScheme: 1 mark: oxygen (air) and water
questions.explanation: Salt speeds up rusting but is not needed. Nitrogen and carbon dioxide are not required.

questions.question: Which method is used to prevent a bicycle chain from rusting?
markScheme: 1 mark: oiling or greasing
questions.explanation: Moving parts need oil or grease; paint would crack off. Copper cannot galvanise and gold plating would be too expensive.

questions.question: Which metal is used to galvanise iron?
markScheme: 1 mark: Zinc
questions.explanation: Galvanising is coating with zinc, which is more reactive than iron. Tin is used for plating food cans but is not galvanising.

questions.question: Why does aluminium not corrode as much as expected from its position in the reactivity series?
options: It is less reactive than iron
It does not react with oxygen
It forms a thin, tough oxide layer that protects it
markScheme: 1 mark: oxide layer protects it
questions.explanation: Aluminium is more reactive than iron, but its oxide coating protects the metal from further corrosion.

questions.question: In the rusting experiment, why is a layer of oil added on top of boiled water?
options: To stop air dissolving into the water
To make the nail rust faster
markScheme: 1 mark: to stop air dissolving into the water
questions.explanation: Boiling removes the dissolved air; the oil layer stops it returning, so the nail has water but no oxygen.

questions.question: Which metal could be attached to a steel ship hull to give sacrificial protection?
markScheme: 1 mark: Magnesium
questions.explanation: Only a metal more reactive than iron gives sacrificial protection. Copper, lead and silver are less reactive than iron.

questions.question: A steel can is plated with tin. The tin is scratched, exposing the steel. What happens?
options: The tin corrodes instead of the iron
The iron rusts, because tin is less reactive than iron and only acts as a barrier
The iron is protected because tin is a sacrificial metal
markScheme: 1 mark: the iron rusts because tin is less reactive and only acts as a barrier
questions.explanation: Tin is below iron in reactivity, so it cannot provide sacrificial protection. In fact the exposed iron corrodes even faster.

questions.question: Which half equation shows what happens to the zinc in sacrificial protection?
markScheme: 1 mark: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻
questions.explanation: Zinc atoms lose electrons (are oxidised) instead of iron atoms. The first option is reduction, and the third has electrons on the wrong side.

questions.question: An iron nail had a mass of 3.40 g. After rusting, its mass was 3.55 g. Calculate the increase in mass.
questions.explanation: The mass increases because oxygen and water combine with the iron.

questions.question: An iron nail had a mass of 4.00 g. After four weeks in salt water its mass was 4.18 g. Calculate the percentage increase in mass.
markScheme: 1 mark: 4.5%

questions.question: A sacrificial zinc block on a ship has a mass of 12 kg. It loses 1.5 kg of zinc each year. Calculate how many years it will take for the block to be used up completely.
markScheme: 1 mark: 8 years
questions.explanation: Time = total mass ÷ mass lost per year = 12 ÷ 1.5 = 8 years. The block must be replaced before then.

questions.question: A student puts identical 5.00 g nails in tap water and in salt water. After 3 weeks, the nail in tap water has a mass of 5.06 g and the nail in salt water has a mass of 5.15 g. Calculate how many times greater the mass increase was in salt water than in tap water.
markScheme: 1 mark: tap water increase = 0.06 g
1 mark: salt water increase = 0.15 g
questions.explanation: Salt speeds up rusting: the mass gain was 2.5 times greater in salt water.

questions.question: A zinc coating on a galvanised fence is 85 μm thick. In a coastal area the zinc corrodes at 3.4 μm per year. Calculate how many years the coating will last.
markScheme: 1 mark: 25 years
questions.explanation: Lifetime = thickness ÷ rate of loss = 85 ÷ 3.4 = 25 years.

questions.question: Name two barrier methods that can be used to prevent iron from rusting.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: painting / greasing or oiling / electroplating
questions.explanation: These stop air and water reaching the iron.

questions.question: State the chemical name for rust.
markScheme: 1 mark: hydrated iron(III) oxide
questions.explanation: Rust forms when iron reacts with oxygen and water.

questions.question: State why anhydrous calcium chloride is placed in one of the test tubes in the rusting experiment.
markScheme: 1 mark: to absorb water (vapour) so the air is dry
questions.explanation: This tests whether iron rusts with air but no water.

questions.question: Explain how painting prevents a steel bridge from rusting.
acceptedAnswers: stops oxygen and water reaching the iron
markScheme: 1 mark: paint acts as a barrier
1 mark: stopping oxygen (air) and water reaching the iron
questions.explanation: Both air and water are needed for rusting, so removing contact with either stops it.

questions.question: Explain how galvanising protects iron, even when the zinc coating is scratched.
markScheme: 1 mark: the zinc coating acts as a barrier to air and water
1 mark: zinc is more reactive than iron
1 mark: so if scratched, zinc reacts/corrodes (is oxidised) instead of the iron (sacrificial protection)
questions.explanation: Galvanising combines a barrier with sacrificial protection.

questions.question: Use ideas about electrons to explain why magnesium blocks protect a steel pipeline from corrosion.
markScheme: 1 mark: magnesium is more reactive so it loses electrons more easily than iron
1 mark: magnesium is oxidised instead of iron, so the iron does not lose electrons / corrode
questions.explanation: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ happens in preference to Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻.

questions.question: Suggest why tin-plated steel food cans rust quickly once they are dented and the coating is broken.
acceptedAnswers: iron exposed to air and water
markScheme: 1 mark: the barrier is broken so iron is exposed to air and water
1 mark: tin is less reactive than iron so does not give sacrificial protection
questions.explanation: Tin protects only as a barrier.

questions.question: Explain why rusting can eventually destroy an iron object completely, whereas aluminium objects stay intact.
markScheme: 1 mark: rust is weak and flakes off, exposing fresh iron to further rusting
1 mark: aluminium oxide forms a tough layer that stays on and protects the metal from further corrosion
questions.explanation: The difference is whether the corrosion product protects or falls away.

questions.question: Describe an experiment to show that both air and water are needed for iron to rust. Include the results you would expect and how each result supports the conclusion.
markScheme: Indicative content: three test tubes each with an iron nail; tube 1 nail in tap water open to air (control); tube 2 nail in boiled water (boiling removes dissolved air) with a layer of oil on top to stop air dissolving; tube 3 nail with anhydrous calcium chloride to absorb water, sealed with a bung; leave for about a week; observe; tube 1 rusts; tube 2 no rust shows air needed; tube 3 no rust shows water needed; use identical nails, same time, same temperature.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): all three set-ups described with purpose of boiling, oil and calcium chloride, correct expected results linked to the conclusion, and control variables.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): at least two set-ups described with some reasons and some results.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple description, for example 'put a nail in water and see if it rusts'.
questions.explanation: Each tube removes one factor; comparing them with the control shows which factors are needed.

questions.question: A company makes steel garden gates. Compare painting and galvanising as ways to prevent the gates from rusting.
markScheme: Indicative content: both act as barriers to air and water; painting is cheap, easy to reapply and can be coloured, but if scratched the iron is exposed and rusts; galvanising coats with zinc, which is more reactive than iron, so gives sacrificial protection even when scratched; galvanising is more expensive initially but longer lasting; zinc coating eventually used up.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear comparison including the barrier idea and sacrificial protection explained using reactivity.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple description of one or both methods.
questions.explanation: The key difference is what happens when the coating is damaged.

questions.question: Give one example of an object that is protected from corrosion by electroplating.
markScheme: 1 mark: for example chromium-plated taps / tin-plated food cans / silver-plated cutlery
questions.explanation: Electroplating gives a thin coating of a metal that resists corrosion.

questions.question: Which change happens to the mass of an iron nail when it rusts?
markScheme: 1 mark: It increases
questions.explanation: Oxygen and water from the environment become part of the rust, so the mass goes up.

questions.question: A student says, 'Copper blocks could be attached to an iron boat to stop it rusting.' Explain why the student is wrong.
markScheme: 1 mark: copper is less reactive than iron
1 mark: so iron would be oxidised/corrode (faster) instead of copper
questions.explanation: Sacrificial protection only works with a more reactive metal such as zinc or magnesium.

questions.question: Iron nails are left for a week in four tubes. Which tube shows the MOST rusting?
options: Nail in dry air with calcium chloride
Nail in boiled water under oil
Nail half in salt water, open to air
markScheme: 1 mark: nail half in salt water, open to air
questions.explanation: Only this tube has both air and water, and salt speeds up rusting.
